lessons.title: What a spreadsheet is for in everyday Canadian life

sections.title: Lists you already keep

blocks.html:
A spreadsheet is a tool for lists and numbers. You may already keep those lists on paper, in a notebook, or in a phone note. A hall volunteer might write hours people worked each day. A farm household might jot down feed, fuel, and grocery amounts in Canadian dollars. Those lists work — until you need a total, a sorted list, or a clear copy to share.

Excel is Microsoft's spreadsheet program. Microsoft's basic-tasks page says it works well for simple calculations and for tracking almost any kind of information. The key is a grid of cells. Each cell can hold a number, text, or a formula. You group cells in rows and columns so you can add the numbers up, sort or filter the list, put it in a table, or show it in a chart.

You do not need a huge file or a finance job. A one-week hours list with seven rows is a real spreadsheet. A five-line household list in CAD is a real spreadsheet too. The grid keeps each piece of information in its own box, so totals and labels stay lined up when you add a row.

The Government of Canada's Skills for Success describe Digital as the ability to use digital tools to find, manage, apply, create, and share information. One official example is creating spreadsheets, and the same page names Excel as a common digital tool. Skills for Success also name Numeracy, which includes checking whether a result makes sense. This course practises both.

A spreadsheet is not magic. If an hours total says you worked 400 hours in one week, the sheet did the math you typed — it did not notice that the number is unlikely. Later lessons will show you how to check a total. For now, the purpose is a clear list, in one place, that you can total and share without rewriting it by hand.

sections.title: Workbooks, sheets, and cells

blocks.html:
Microsoft calls an Excel file a workbook. A workbook holds one or more sheets (people also say spreadsheets or worksheets). You can add more sheets to the same workbook, or start a new workbook to keep one set of information separate. A good habit is one workbook for one purpose — for example a hall hours file, not a mix of hours, recipes, and a neighbour's phone numbers.

Each sheet is a grid. Columns have letters (A, B, C). Rows have numbers (1, 2, 3). A cell is one box where a column and a row meet. Microsoft's basic-tasks page uses this example: cell A1 is in the first row of column A. Cell B9 is column B, row 9. That address is how you and Excel name a place on the sheet.

A cell can hold:

  • Text, such as Mon, Community hall setup, or Milk 2 litre.
  • A number, such as 6 hours or 5.49 dollars.
  • A formula, an instruction that starts with = and asks Excel to calculate something. You will write formulas later.

The sheet tabs sit along the bottom of the window. Your practice workbook has three tabs: Hours, Household, and Practice. The active cell — the one you are working in — has a thicker border. When you type, the text also appears in the formula bar near the top. That bar is useful later, when a cell shows a total and you want to read the formula behind it.

You do not have to fill the whole sheet. Empty cells are fine. What matters is that each column has one kind of information (a day, an amount, a note) and each row is one item or one day. That layout lets Excel add, sort, and chart your list later.

sections.title: What this course will teach — and what it will not

blocks.html:
This is a basics course. You will open a workbook, move around the grid, type text, numbers, and dates, and format a list so other people can read it. You will write simple formulas that start with =, use AutoSum and AVERAGE, fill or copy a formula, and lock a cell reference when it should stay put. You will sort and filter a list, make a simple table, make a basic chart, and save, print, or export a PDF without sharing private information.

This course will not teach PivotTables, Power Query, macros, or advanced analysis. Those skills are useful later, but they are not the everyday starting point. We stay with the skills most learners need first.

This course is also not tax help, payroll help, or bookkeeping training. When a later lesson uses a sample extra-rate column (for example a GST-style extra on a household amount), the rate is a practice number only. It is not the rate you must use, and it is not advice for your tax return or your pay. Sample hours and pay-stub-style figures are examples too.

You do not need to buy a new computer. A home, work, library, or council machine with Excel is enough. Excel for the web can be a backup, but some tools (such as Quick Analysis on Windows desktop) may look different or may not appear. If a button is missing, use the matching ribbon command this course also names.

There is no video. Each click-path has written steps and an interactive walk-through. Lesson quizzes are practice, not a mark. The graded finish line is the final exam after Lesson 10.

sections.title: Worked example 1. A week of hall hours on paper vs in a sheet

blocks.title: Worked example 1. A week of hall hours on paper vs in a sheet

blocks.html:
Pat helps set up the community hall. On paper the week is: Mon 6 hours, Tue 4, Wed 7.5, Thu off, Fri 5, Sat 3, Sun off. Added up, that is 25.5 hours. If Pat later remembers that Friday was 5.5, not 5, the whole addition has to be done again, and anyone who received a paper copy still has the old total.

In Excel, that same week is the Hours sheet: days in column A, hours in column B, and a short note in column C. When you learn AutoSum, you will put a total in cell B9. If Friday changes, the total can update. That is the everyday reason to use a sheet: it is easy to correct and easy to share a clear copy.

sections.title: Worked example 2. A small household list in CAD

blocks.title: Worked example 2. A small household list in CAD

blocks.html:
A farm household writes five lines: milk (2 litre) at the Co-op for $5.49, bread at the Co-op for $3.29, fuel at the cardlock for $80.00, feed at the farm supply for $45.00, and a phone card at the hardware store for $25.00. On paper the total is $158.78.

In the Household sheet, each item has its own row: item (with the Canadian spelling *litre*), store, amount in CAD, and a category such as Groceries or Vehicle. Later you will total column C, format the amounts so they line up like money, filter to see only Groceries, and make a simple chart. The data stays the same five lines — stored in a grid so Excel can help.

lessons.title: Open a workbook and move around the grid

sections.title: Start a blank workbook

blocks.html:
Before you type anything, you need a workbook — the Excel file that will hold your sheets. Microsoft's basic-tasks page gives a short path for a new file:

  1. Click File, and then click New.
  2. Under New, click Blank workbook.

A new window opens with an empty grid. The sheet is usually named Sheet1. Cell A1 is selected. That empty grid is a good place to practise moving around before you open the sample file that already has data in it.

If Excel is not yet open, start it from the Start menu (Windows) or the Applications folder or Dock (Mac), then use File > New > Blank workbook. On some computers a start screen already shows Blank workbook as a large tile. Clicking that tile does the same job as the File path above. Screens look a little different in Excel for the web and on a Mac, but you are still looking for New and Blank workbook.

If you work on a library or council computer, you may need to sign in or choose a Microsoft 365 account first. Ask the person who looks after that computer if a sign-in screen appears and you are not sure which account to use. Do not save practice files with someone else's personal information on a shared machine.

You can have more than one workbook open at a time. Each workbook is its own file. Later, when you save, you will choose a folder and a file name so you can find the file again. Saving is Lesson 10. For this lesson it is enough to create the blank file and practise moving around. If the computer asks you to save when you close, you can save a practice copy with a clear name such as excel-moving-practice or close without saving if you only clicked around.

sections.title: Read the window: columns, rows, and the active cell

blocks.html:
Once the blank workbook is open, pause and look at the frame around the grid. Across the top of the grid are column letters: A, B, C. Down the left side are row numbers: 1, 2, 3. Cell A1 sits at the top-left corner. Microsoft's basic-tasks page reminds you that cells are named by that location: A1 is column A, row 1.

The active cell is the one with the thicker border. That is where the next thing you type will go. In the top-left area, a small box called the name box usually shows the active cell's address (A1 when you start). To the right of the name box is the formula bar, a longer strip that shows what is in the active cell. When the cell is empty, the formula bar is empty too.

The ribbon is the band of buttons across the top of the window. In this course you will use the Home tab often (for borders, fill colour, AutoSum, and number formats), and later the Formulas, Insert, Data, and File tabs. You do not need to learn every button. When a lesson needs a button, it will name the tab and the group.

Along the bottom are sheet tabs. A new workbook usually starts with one tab called Sheet1. Your practice file has three named tabs: Hours, Household, and Practice. Clicking a tab switches sheets. The workbook is still the same file; you are only looking at a different page inside it.

If the window feels crowded, you can scroll with the bars on the right and bottom, or with a mouse wheel or trackpad. Scrolling does not change the active cell. It only changes what you can see. If you click a cell after scrolling, that new cell becomes active. Watch the name box to confirm where you are.

sections.title: Move from cell to cell

blocks.html:
Microsoft's basic-tasks page says that after you type in a cell you press Enter or Tab to move to the next cell. Those two keys do not move the same way:

  • Enter (Return on a Mac) usually moves the selection down, to the cell below.
  • Tab moves the selection to the right, to the next column.

You can also click any cell with the mouse or trackpad, or press the arrow keys to move one cell at a time up, down, left, or right. For a small list, arrows and clicks are often the calmest way to move. For typing down a column of hours, Enter is handy because it drops you into the next day's row. For typing across a header row (Day, Hours worked, Notes), Tab is handy because it moves you along the row.

Try this on a blank sheet without worrying about content: click A1, press Tab (you should land on B1), press Tab again (C1), then press Enter (often C2), then use the left arrow to walk back. Watch the thick border and the name box each time. If you get lost, click A1 or type A1 in the name box and press Enter to jump back to the corner.

To open a file you already have, such as the practice workbook, use File > Open and browse to the file. (Microsoft's save page later uses File for Save and Save As; Open lives on the same File tab.) If you cannot find the practice file, you can still do this lesson in a blank workbook and type a few labels of your own.

sections.title: Type text and move to the next cell

blocks.html:
Microsoft's basic-tasks page gives three steps for entering data:

  1. Click an empty cell. For example, click A1 on a new sheet.
  2. Type text or a number in the cell.
  3. Press Enter or Tab to move to the next cell.

That is the whole habit. Click, type, confirm. If you click away with the mouse instead of pressing a key, Excel usually keeps what you typed as well. If a cell still shows the old value, click it once and look at the formula bar. If your new text is not there, click the cell and type again, then press Enter.

Text is anything Excel should not add up: Day, Mon, Community hall setup, Milk 2 litre, Co-op. Headers belong in row 1 so every column has a name. Short labels are easier to read than long sentences. You can write a longer note in a Notes column when you need it.

If the text is wider than the column, the extra letters may spill visually into the next cell — or they may look cut off if the next cell has its own content. The full text is still in the cell. Click it and read the formula bar. In Lesson 4 you will widen a column so the sheet is easier to read. For now, do not worry if a long note looks cramped.

Use the Practice sheet for experiments so you do not overwrite the sample Hours or Household lists until a task asks you to. If you type in the wrong cell on those sample sheets, click that cell and type the sample value again from the workbook layout at the start of this course.

sections.title: Type numbers — and keep units in the header

blocks.html:
Numbers are values Excel can calculate later: 6, 7.5, 5.49, 80, 0. Type them without extra words in the same cell. Put the unit in the header instead. Write Hours worked in B1 and 6 in B2, not 6 hours in B2. Write Amount (CAD) in C1 and 5.49 in C2, not five dollars forty-nine and not $5.49 CAD mixed with words. You will learn number formats (including a currency look) in Lesson 4. A clean number is easier for AutoSum to add.

Use a decimal point for parts of an hour or parts of a dollar, as in 7.5 and 5.49. Do not type a space in the middle of a number. If you type 7,5 Excel may treat that as text or as a thousands style, depending on the computer's region settings. On most Canadian English computers, 7.5 is the safe way to type seven and a half.

A zero and a blank are not the same. On the Hours sheet, Thursday is 0 because that day was off — you recorded “no hours.” A blank cell means nothing has been entered yet. When you total a column later, you will want recorded days off to stay as 0 so the row is not mistaken for missing data.

If a number looks left-aligned like a word, Excel may have stored it as text (for example if you typed 6 hours). Lesson 6 will ask you to check that a total makes sense. A first defence is to keep numbers as numbers from the start.

sections.title: Type a date and fix a mistake

blocks.html:
Excel can store a date as a date, not just as decoration. When it does, you can format how the date looks without typing it again. Microsoft's number-format help says you apply a format from the Home tab: select the cell, then choose a format from the Number drop-down (the box that often starts as General). Microsoft's basic-tasks page describes the same idea: click the arrow in the General box and pick a format, or choose More Number Formats if you do not see the one you want. Date is one of the formats in that list.

To change only part of a long note, click the cell, click inside the formula bar, edit the words, and press Enter. lessons.title: Format cells so a list is easy to read

sections.title: Format for readers — not for decoration

blocks.html:
A list is easier to trust when other people can see where one row ends and the next begins, and when money looks like money. Formatting is that extra clarity. Microsoft's basic-tasks page covers three everyday tools you will use here: cell borders, cell shading (fill colour), and number formats such as currency, percentages, or dates.

Number formats change how a value is displayed. They do not change the value itself. Microsoft's number-format help says this plainly: formats only change how numbers appear and do not affect the values. If cell C2 contains 5.49 and you apply a Currency format, the cell may show something like $5.49, but Excel still stores 5.49 for any later formula. That is why you typed plain numbers in Lesson 3.

Good formatting is calm. A bold-looking header row (a light fill and a bottom border) helps. A thin border around the data block helps. Matching decimal places in a money column helps. Rainbow colours, a different fill on every row, or a tiny font do not help. If you use colour, use it as a backup to clear labels, not as the only way to tell categories apart — a print-out or a photocopy may lose the colour.

You do not need to format empty rows below the list. Format the cells you are actually using, including the header row. If you add a new row later, you can copy the format from a neighbour cell or select the new cells and apply the same border and number format again.

blocks.html:
Microsoft's steps for a border are:

  1. Select the cell or range you want to add a border to.
  2. On the Home tab, in the Font group, click the arrow next to Borders, and then click the border style you want.

A useful style for a small list is All Borders around the block that has data, or a bottom border under the header row. Select a range by clicking the first cell and dragging to the last cell. To use the keyboard, Microsoft says to hold down Shift while you press the arrow keys.

Microsoft's steps for shading are:

  1. Select the cell or range.
  2. On the Home tab, in the Font group, choose the arrow next to Fill Color, and then under Theme Colors or Standard Colors, select the colour you want.

A pale fill on the header row (A1:C1 on Hours, or A1:D1 on Household) is enough. Avoid very dark fills that hide black text. If you colour a cell by mistake, open Fill Color again and choose No Fill if that option appears, or pick white.

Select first, then click the tool. If you click Borders or Fill Color with only one cell selected, only that cell changes. If you meant to format the whole list, select the full block and apply the style again.

Border menus often list more than one style (for example a bottom border, outside borders, or all borders). For a small everyday list, all borders — lines around and between the cells — usually make the grid easiest to follow on screen and on paper. If the result looks too heavy, choose a simpler style and try the range again.

lessons.title: Write a simple formula that starts with =

sections.title: A formula always starts with =

blocks.html:
A formula is an instruction that tells Excel to calculate. Microsoft's formula pages repeat one rule: a formula always begins with an equal sign (=). If you type 2+4 without the equal sign, Excel usually treats it as text — it will not give you 6. If you type =2+4 and press Enter, Excel runs the calculation and the cell shows 6. The formula bar still shows =2+4, so you can see how the answer was made.

Microsoft's simple-formula page says a simple formula starts with =, then numbers (constants) and operators:

  • + add
  • - subtract
  • * multiply (asterisk, not the letter x)
  • / divide (forward slash)

Their starter examples are =2+4, =4-2, =2*4, and =4/2. You can type those on the Practice sheet right now. After you press Enter (Windows) or Return (Mac), the cell shows the result. Microsoft also notes that you can press Ctrl+Enter if you want the cursor to stay on the active cell after the formula calculates.

Type the equal sign first, then the rest. If you forget = and already pressed Enter, click the cell, type the formula again starting with =, and press Enter. Watch the formula bar, not only the grid, when you want to know whether a cell holds a formula or a typed-in number.

You can practise these tiny formulas on the Practice sheet without touching the sample Hours or Household data. Use a clear empty area, such as row 10 downward, so your tests do not sit on top of headers.

Progress: Lesson 5, part 2 of 3.

sections.title: Point the formula at other cells

blocks.html:
Adding =2+4 is a good first test, but everyday lists change. If Wednesday's hours change from 7.5 to 8, a formula that literally says =6+4+7.5 will be wrong until you edit it. A better habit is to point at the cells that already hold the numbers.

Microsoft's overview shows this pattern: select a cell, type =, select a cell (or type its address), type an operator, select the next cell, and press Enter. The result appears in the cell that holds the formula. Microsoft's simple-formula page adds that instead of typing the numbers, you can select the cells that contain the values and type the operators between those selections.

On the Hours sheet, click an empty cell such as E2 and type =B2+B3+B4, or type =, click B2, type +, click B3, type +, click B4, and press Enter. If the sample data is unchanged, the result is 17.5 (Monday 6 + Tuesday 4 + Wednesday 7.5). If you later change B4 from 7.5 to 8, this formula can update to 18.

Microsoft's overview also says it is generally best to put constants in their own cells and refer to those cells, rather than burying numbers inside a formula. That habit will matter even more in Lesson 7, when you copy a formula down a column.

If the result looks like a date or a long string of hash marks, the cell may be too narrow or formatted strangely. Click the cell, read the formula bar, and confirm the cell references before you change anything else.

sections.title: Multiply and divide before you add and subtract

blocks.html:
Excel follows the standard order of mathematical operations. Microsoft's simple-formula page states that multiplication and division are performed before addition and subtraction. Their example is to type =5+2*3 and press Enter. Excel multiplies the last two numbers (2 × 3 = 6) and then adds the first number (5 + 6). The result is 11, not 21.

This matters in real lists. Suppose you want to add two hour totals and then multiply by a sample extra rate later in the course. If you write the operators in a long line, Excel will not always go left to right. Read the formula bar and do a rough check in your head: “Which part happens first?” If the on-screen answer is far from your estimate, look at the operators before you trust the cell.

This course stays with the four everyday operators Microsoft teaches for simple formulas: add, subtract, multiply, and divide. You do not need more advanced operators to finish the practice workbook. What you do need is the habit of starting with =, pointing at cells when the numbers already live on the sheet, and checking that 11-versus-21 kind of surprise.

If a formula shows an error such as #DIV/0!, you may have divided by a cell that is empty or zero. Click the formula cell, read the formula bar, and fix the cell references rather than typing over the result with a guessed number. The displayed result should come from the formula.

sections.title: AutoSum — a fast way to add a column or row

blocks.html:
When numbers are already in a column or a row, Microsoft offers AutoSum so you do not have to type =B2+B3+B4+... by hand. The basic-tasks page says:

  1. Select the cell to the right of, or below, the numbers you want to add.
  2. Click the Home tab, and then click AutoSum in the Editing group.
  3. AutoSum adds the numbers and shows the result in the cell you selected.

The simple-formula page gives the same idea and adds that AutoSum is also on the Formulas tab. When you select AutoSum, Excel enters a formula that uses the SUM function and highlights the cells it plans to total. You press Enter (Windows) or Return (Mac) to accept. On Windows, Microsoft also lists the shortcut Alt+= , which inserts SUM.

To total a column, select the cell immediately below the last number. To total a row, select the cell immediately to the right. On the Hours sheet, that means clicking B9 (under Sunday's hours) and using AutoSum. With the sample data, Excel should propose something like =SUM(B2:B8). After you press Enter, the result is 25.5 hours (6+4+7.5+0+5+3+0).

Look at the proposed range before you press Enter. If AutoSum highlighted the wrong cells — for example if it included a label — drag to correct the selection or edit the range in the formula bar, then press Enter. The colon in B2:B8 means “from B2 through B8.”

sections.title: AVERAGE — typical value of a group of numbers

blocks.html:
Excel can also calculate an average (the mean): add the numbers, then divide by how many numbers were included. Microsoft's “Calculate an average” page shows this path:

  1. Select the cells you want to average, *or* select the cell where the average should appear.
  2. On the Formulas tab, select the arrow next to AutoSum, and then select Average.

When you create the average in its own cell, the formula bar shows a function that looks like =AVERAGE(A2:A7) in Microsoft's sample. On the Hours sheet, click B11 (leaving a blank row under the total is fine) or another empty cell, choose Formulas > AutoSum arrow > Average, and check that the range points at the hours, B2:B8, not at the total in B9. If AutoSum's average includes the total, the answer will be too high. Edit the range so it covers only the days.

With the sample hours 6, 4, 7.5, 0, 5, 3, and 0, the average is 25.5 ÷ 7, which is about 3.64 hours per day if every listed day counts — including Thursday and Sunday as zeros. That is mathematically correct for “average of the seven recorded days.” It is not the same as “average of only the days I worked.” If you need the second meaning, you would average only the working days (or leave days off out of the sheet). This course does not teach extra functions that ignore certain values. What it teaches is to read the range inside AVERAGE and know which cells are included.

You can also type =AVERAGE(B2:B8) yourself, the same way you typed =SUM(B2:B8). Starting with = and using a colon range is the same habit as Lesson 5, with a function name added. Microsoft's overview of formulas shows that pattern: type =, a function name, (, the range, then ).

sections.title: Check that the answer makes sense

blocks.html:
A formula will calculate exactly what you asked — even if you asked for the wrong range. Skills for Success describe Numeracy as including interpreting and evaluating information, and they give this kind of check: see whether the answer is of the expected size. That habit belongs beside AutoSum and AVERAGE, not after a mistake has already been shared.

Before you accept 25.5 as the week's hours, estimate. Monday through Saturday without a calculator is roughly 6 + 4 + 8 + 0 + 5 + 3 + 0, which is about 26. 25.5 is close, so it is plausible. If AutoSum showed 255 or 7.5, something would be wrong: a decimal in the wrong place, a range that grabbed the wrong cells, or a number typed as text.

Checks that catch many everyday mistakes:

  • Read the formula bar. Does =SUM(B2:B8) start at the first day and stop before the total cell?
  • Compare SUM to a rough mental total.
  • Remember that zeros count in both SUM and AVERAGE. They do not change the sum, but they do pull an average down.
  • If a total looks like a date, the cell may have the wrong number format (Lesson 4). Set it back to Number or General.
  • If SUM ignores a number, that number may have been typed as text (6 hours). Type a plain number instead.

Do not type over a formula result with a number you calculated by hand unless you intend to remove the formula. If you type 25.5 into B9, the cell will no longer update when Friday's hours change.

lessons.title: Fill, copy, and when a cell reference should stay put

sections.title: Fill a formula into the cells beside it

blocks.html:
Once one formula works, you should not have to retype it on every row. Microsoft's fill page says you can copy formulas into adjacent cells by dragging the fill handle — the small square at the corner of the selected cell. Select the cell that has the formula, then drag the fill handle across the cells you want to fill. When you fill down, relative references adjust for each row, unless you used an absolute or mixed reference first.

If you do not see the fill handle, Microsoft says it may be hidden. On Windows desktop Excel, display it again with File > Options > Advanced, and under Editing Options check Enable fill handle and cell drag-and-drop. After you drag, a small Auto Fill Options icon may appear so you can change how the fill worked.

You can also fill without dragging:

  1. Select the cell with the formula and the adjacent cells you want to fill.
  2. Select Home > Fill, and choose Down, Right, Up, or Left.

Microsoft also lists keyboard shortcuts: Ctrl+D fills down a column, and Ctrl+R fills to the right in a row. On Excel for the web, Microsoft describes dragging the fill handle or using those same shortcuts.

If a filled formula shows the old result and does not change, automatic calculation may be off. Microsoft's fill page says to choose File > Options > Formulas and, under Calculation options, set Workbook Calculation to Automatic. You do not need to change this if your formulas already update when you press Enter.

sections.title: Relative references move with the formula

blocks.html:
By default, a cell reference is relative. Microsoft explains it this way: when you refer to A2 from C2, you are referring to a cell two columns left and in the same row. If you copy =A2+B2 from C2 to C3, the references shift down one row and become =A3+B3. The overview page gives another picture: if you copy a relative reference in B2 that points at A1 down to B3, it adjusts from =A1 to =A2.

That is why filling =C15*2 from D15 to D16 becomes =C16*2. Excel assumes you want “twice *this* row's amount,” not “twice the first amount, over and over.” For hours, a relative formula on each row is usually what you want.

Relative references are helpful — and they can surprise you. If cell H1 holds a sample extra rate and you write =C2*H1 in E2, that works on row 2. If you fill it down to E3, the formula becomes =C3*H2. H2 is probably empty, so the result may be 0 or look blank. The formula did not “break” at random. It moved H1 down one row because H1 was relative. Lesson 7's next chapter shows how to stop that move.

When something looks wrong after a fill, click each result cell and read the formula bar. Ask: “Did every reference shift the way I meant?” If one reference should have stayed on H1, that reference needs to be locked.

Progress: Lesson 7, part 3 of 3.

sections.title: Lock a cell with $ when it should stay put

blocks.html:
If you want a reference to stay on one cell when you copy or fill, Microsoft says you “lock” it by putting a dollar sign ($) before the column letter and the row number. That is an absolute reference. Their example: if you copy =$A$2+$B$2 from C2 to D2, the formula stays exactly the same. The overview page uses $A$1 as the pattern: copy or fill it and it still points at A1.

Microsoft also describes mixed references, which lock only the column ($A2) or only the row (B$3). Those are less common in a short everyday list. This course only asks you to lock both parts when one input — such as a single sample rate — should be used on every row: $H$1.

To change a reference, Microsoft says to select the cell that contains the formula, click the reference in the formula bar, and then use the keyboard shortcut shown in your Excel version to cycle the $ signs — or simply type the $ characters yourself. Typing $H$1 is enough for this course and works the same on Windows, Mac, and the web.

Use this power carefully with money. A later try-it will put a sample extra rate such as 0.05 in one cell and multiply household amounts by it. That rate is a practice number only. It is not tax advice, not a CRA rule, and not the extra you must charge or pay. Do not treat the result as GST, payroll, or a real invoice. (Any specific public rate can change; we keep the number inside a labelled sample cell and out of the quizzes.)

lessons.title: Sort, filter, and a simple table

sections.title: Sort a list without breaking the rows

blocks.html:
Sorting rearranges rows so you can read a list in order — A to Z, Z to A, smallest number to largest, or the reverse. Microsoft's basic-tasks page describes two approaches. For a sort with specific choices, select a single cell anywhere in the range, then on the Data tab, in the Sort & Filter group, choose Sort. A Sort dialog appears. In Sort by, pick the first column to sort on. In Sort On, choose Values (you can also see Cell Color, Font Color, or Cell Icon — this course stays with Values). In Order, choose A to Z or Z to A for text, or smallest to largest / largest to smallest for numbers.

Before you sort, select a range that includes every column of the list, or click inside a well-formed block that has headers. Microsoft's example ranges include several columns at once (such as A1:L5) as well as a single column. For the Household sheet, that means keeping Item, Store, Amount, and Category together. If you sort only the Amount column, the prices can detach from the item names. That is one of the easiest ways to ruin a list. If a sort looks wrong, use Undo if you still can, or go back to the sample layout at the start of this course.

On Hours, you might sort by hours (largest first) to see which day was busiest. Wednesday's 7.5 hours should still travel with the note “Market stall.” After you finish looking, you can sort Day back to the original week order if you need Monday through Sunday again — or keep a copy of the file before you experiment.

Progress: Lesson 8, part 2 of 3.

sections.title: Filter so only some rows show

blocks.html:
Filtering hides rows that do not match your choice. The rows are still in the workbook; they are just not shown until you clear the filter. Microsoft's basic-tasks steps are:

  1. Select the data you want to filter.
  2. On the Data tab, in the Sort & Filter group, click Filter.
  3. Click the arrow in a column header to see the choices.
  4. To select by values, clear the (Select All) check box, select only the values you want to see, and click OK.

On Household, click inside A1:D6, choose Data > Filter, then click the arrow on Category. Clear Select All, tick Groceries, and click OK. Only Milk 2 litre and Bread should remain visible (5.49 and 3.29). Fuel, feed, and the phone card are hidden, not deleted. To see everything again, open the same arrow and choose Select All, or turn Filter off from the Data tab.

You can set a filter on more than one header. For example, you might first show only the Co-op in Store, then look at Category. Each extra filter hides more rows. If the sheet looks “too empty,” open each header arrow and see what is still ticked.

Filters are helpful before a meeting: “Show me only Vehicle costs” or “Show me only the Co-op.” They are not a good place to hide private information you should have removed. Hidden rows can still travel with the file when you share it (Lesson 10). Use filter to read a list, not to conceal something sensitive.

sections.title: Turn the list into a simple table

blocks.html:
Microsoft's basic-tasks page says a simple way to use Excel's power is to put data in a table, which lets you quickly filter or sort. One official Windows desktop path uses Quick Analysis:

  1. Select your data by clicking the first cell and dragging to the last cell (or hold Shift and use the arrow keys).
  2. Click the Quick Analysis button in the bottom-right corner of the selection.
  3. Click Tables, preview the Table button, and then click Table.
  4. Use the arrow in a table header to filter (clear Select All, then tick what you want) or to sort A to Z / Z to A.

Microsoft notes Quick Analysis in that article in connection with Excel 2016. If you do not see the Quick Analysis button (common on some Mac setups and on Excel for the web), use the path on Microsoft's create-and-format-tables page instead:

  1. Select a cell within your data.
  2. Select Home > Format as Table.
  3. Choose a style.
  4. In the Create Table dialog, check the cell range.
  5. Mark whether your table has headers.
  6. Select OK.

A table keeps header arrows ready for sort and filter and applies a readable style. For this basics course, that is enough. You do not need PivotTables, slicers, or Power Query. If Excel asks “Does your table have headers?”, say yes when row 1 already contains words such as Item, Store, Amount (CAD), and Category. If you say no, Excel may add names like Column1.

sections.title: Choose the cells — and a simple chart type

blocks.html:
A chart is a picture of numbers that already live on the sheet. It does not invent new facts. If Wednesday is 7.5 hours in the grid, the bar or column for Wednesday should match 7.5. Microsoft's chart page says charts help you visualize data, and it starts with a plain instruction: select the data for the chart, then choose a chart.

Select the labels and the numbers together. For a week of hours, select A1:B8 — the Day header and values, and the Hours worked header and values. If you select only the numbers, the chart may show 1, 2, 3 instead of Mon, Tue, Wed. If you include the Total row (row 9) by accident, the total can dwarf the days and make the picture misleading. Select through Sunday only unless you truly want the total in the chart.

This course stays with everyday types. Microsoft describes column charts as a common way to show categories along the horizontal axis and values up the vertical axis — a good fit for hours by day. Pie charts show parts of one whole. Microsoft says to consider a pie when you have only one data series, none of the values are negative, almost none are zero, and you have no more than seven categories that really are parts of the same total. Five household amounts can make a pie; a week with two zero days is a weaker pie (those slices vanish) and a better column chart.

You do not need 3-D exploding pies, trendlines, or combination charts here. A flat column chart with a clear title is enough. Give the chart a title that names the list and reminds readers it is sample data, such as Hours worked — sample only.

  4. If you do not see one you like, select the All Charts tab.

Microsoft also notes that you can select the data and press Alt+F1 to create a chart immediately, but it might not be the best chart for the data. Prefer Recommended Charts so you can preview first.

After the chart appears, click it. Extra chart tools show on the ribbon (names can include Chart Design). If a “Chart Title” box is sitting on the chart, click it and type your own title. Screens differ on Mac and on Excel for the web. Microsoft's web instructions still start the same way: select the range, go to the Insert tab, and choose a chart type under Charts. Recommended Charts may appear there for some Microsoft 365 subscribers. If Insert > Recommended Charts is missing, use Insert > Charts and pick a simple column chart.

Keep the chart on the same sheet as the data so you can see both at once and compare them. If you change Friday from 5 to 5.5, glance at the Friday column: it should grow. If it does not, you may have selected the wrong cells when you created the chart.

sections.title: Save on purpose — AutoRecovery is not enough

blocks.html:
Wherever you want to keep a workbook, Microsoft says you do the saving from the File tab. To save an existing workbook in its current place, use Save or press Ctrl+S. To save for the first time, to save in a different place, or to make a copy, use Save As.

Microsoft's first-time Save As steps are:

  1. Click File > Save As.
  2. Under Save As, pick where you want to save the workbook (for example Computer, then Browse to a folder). Microsoft also describes OneDrive as a place you can pick if you use it.
  3. In the File name box, enter a name.
  4. Click Save.

Choose a clear name you will recognise in a week, such as hall-hours-practice-sample-only.xlsx, rather than Book1. On a shared library or council computer, save only to the location staff tell you to use, and do not leave someone else's personal information in the file.

Excel can also store AutoRecovery information while you work. Microsoft's save page says this is not the same as you saving the workbook, and you should not rely on it. Save often with Save or Ctrl+S. To confirm AutoRecovery is on: File > Options, click Save, and make sure Save AutoRecover information every n minutes is checked. That backup is a safety net for a crash or a power cut. It does not replace a file you meant to keep.

sections.title: Preview, print, or export a PDF

blocks.html:
To print, Microsoft's basic-tasks page says: click File, then Print, or press Ctrl+P. Preview the pages with the Next Page and Previous Page arrows before you send anything to the printer. The preview follows your printer settings (black and white or colour). If the pages look wrong, change margins or page breaks rather than printing several wasted copies. Then click Print.

A one-week hours list should usually fit on a page if columns are not extremely wide. If a column spills onto a second almost-blank page, go back and look at the preview — do not assume the paper will “just work.”

To share a copy that looks the same on many computers, Microsoft's Office PDF help says you can save or convert to PDF from the desktop apps without extra software. For Excel on Windows it lists:

  1. Select the File tab.
  2. Select Save As or Save a Copy.
  3. Enter a file name if needed.
  4. In the Save as type list, select **PDF (*.pdf)**.
  5. Optional: choose Standard (for print quality) or Minimum size (when file size matters more), and use Options if you need to control what is included.
  6. Select Save.

Microsoft also warns that sharing something as a PDF is not enough to guarantee the recipient cannot edit the file. Many programs can open a PDF. A PDF is a handy snapshot, not a lock. Microsoft further notes that converting a spreadsheet to PDF drops internal links inside the sheet; external links are another matter. For this course, the practical point is simpler: a PDF still contains the words and numbers you typed. It is not a way to hide a SIN, an account number, or a home address.

sections.title: Share less than you think you need to

blocks.html:
Get Cyber Safe (Public Safety Canada) reminds people to be careful about information they share, even when it seems small. Their advice includes keeping private details such as a home address or phone number private, sharing only when you know why the information is needed, sharing as little as possible, and not storing sensitive details when they are not needed. Before you share anything, they suggest asking who will see it, whether it gives away sensitive information, and why it needs to be shared.

Those questions fit an Excel file as well as a social-media post. A workbook can hold many sheets, hidden rows (Lesson 8), and notes that never appear in a chart. Before you email a file, post it, or hand a USB stick to someone, do a slow check:

  • Open every sheet tab, not just the one you were using.
  • Look at Notes columns, header rows, and cells off to the side (a rate, a name, a comment).
  • Search your eye down for a Social Insurance Number, health number, bank or card number, password, login, or a home address you would not print on a public notice.
  • If the list was filtered, clear the filter and look again. Hidden rows still travel with the file.
  • Ask whether the other person needs the live workbook or only a printed page or PDF of one table.
  • Use sample or made-up practice numbers in this course — never a real person's pay, and never your own private identifiers “just to see how it looks.”

Skills for Success Digital includes storing files in a logical way and applying safe, responsible practices, including protecting personal information. This lesson is that habit in spreadsheet form. It is not a full privacy-law course and not a substitute for your workplace rules. When in doubt, share less, or ask the person who asked for the file which columns they actually need.

There is no video and no live instructor here. If you get stuck on Save As or Print on a library machine, ask the staff who look after that computer, and point them at Microsoft's save and print pages listed at the end of this lesson.

sections.title: Capstone

blocks.html:
This capstone sits after Lesson 10. It pulls the course together: enter a list, write formulas, format money, save, and preview or export — without treating the numbers as real pay.

This is not a pay stub, not payroll, and not tax advice. Use sample numbers only. Do not type a real person's name, Social Insurance Number, address, or real wage.

### What to build

Add a new sheet named Capstone, or start a new workbook. Match this layout:

| | A | B | C | D | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | SAMPLE ONLY — not a real pay stub, not payroll advice, and not tax advice | | | | | 2 | Week of (sample date) | 2026-11-10 | | | | 3 | Day | Hours worked | Sample gross (CAD, example only) | Notes | | 4 | Mon | 6 | *(formula)* | Community hall setup | | 5 | Tue | 4 | *(formula)* | Office desk | | 6 | Wed | 7.5 | *(formula)* | Market stall | | 7 | Thu | 0 | *(formula)* | Day off | | 8 | Fri | 5 | *(formula)* | Library shift | | 9 | Sat | 3 | *(formula)* | Extra shift | | 10 | Sun | 0 | *(formula)* | Day off | | 11 | Total | *(SUM)* | *(SUM)* | |

Off to the side:

  • F1: Sample hourly amount (CAD, example only) — not a real wage
  • F2: 18 (a practice number only)

Tasks:

  1. Type the labels and the seven day rows (you may copy the Hours sheet notes).
  2. In C4 enter =B4*$F$2 and fill down through C10 so every row uses the same sample hourly amount.
  3. In B11 enter =SUM(B4:B10). In C11 enter =SUM(C4:C10).
  4. Format C4:C11 and F2 as Currency (or Number with two decimal places). Format B4:B11 as Number with one decimal place if you like.
  5. Add a pale header fill and borders around A3:D11 so the list is easy to read.
  6. Optional: insert a column chart of Day and Hours (A3:B10) titled Hours worked — sample only. Do not include the Total row in the chart.
  7. File > Save As with a name such as capstone-hours-sample-only.xlsx.
  8. Open File > Print and preview, or File > Save As > PDF (*.pdf) and open the PDF.
  9. Check every sheet tab for anything you would not put on a public notice. There should be no real identifiers.

### Self-check / model answer

Formulas

  • C4 should read =B4*$F$2 (then C5 =B5*$F$2, and so on through C10).
  • B11 should read =SUM(B4:B10).
  • C11 should read =SUM(C4:C10).

Results with the sample hours and the practice amount 18

Sense-check: 25.5 hours times 18 is 459. If C11 is not 459, read each formula bar and confirm $F$2 did not shift to F3, F4, and so on.

Is not, by itself, a guarantee the recipient cannot edit the file
Deletes hidden rows from the original workbook

quiz.explain: Microsoft's PDF warning.

quiz.prompt: Before you email a workbook, you should:

choices.text: Check every sheet tab and look for private details you do not need to send
Add your password in cell A1 so the other person can see it
Filter away sensitive rows and assume they will not be shared

quiz.explain: Open every tab; do not rely on a filter to hide private rows.

quiz.prompt: Get Cyber Safe advice applied here includes:

choices.text: Share as much as possible so nothing is missed
Share only when you know why the information is needed, and share as little as possible
Post account numbers in a chart title

quiz.explain: Know why you are sharing, and share as little as you can.

assignment.title: A one-week hours-and-pay-stub-style list (sample only)
assignment.html: Build the Capstone sheet described in this lesson. Use sample numbers only. This is not a real pay stub and not payroll or tax advice.
tasks: Type the seven day rows and the sample hourly amount 18 in F2 (example only, not a real wage)
In C4 enter =B4*$F$2 and fill down through C10
In B11 enter =SUM(B4:B10) and in C11 enter =SUM(C4:C10)
Format the sample gross column as Currency (or Number with two decimal places)
Save As with a clear name such as capstone-hours-sample-only.xlsx, then preview (File > Print) or export a PDF
Check every sheet tab for anything you would not put on a public notice
assignment.answerKey: With the sample hours and the practice amount 18, B11 is 25.5 and C11 is 459.00 (because 25.5 × 18 = 459). Each gross formula should still mention $F$2. The file has a clear name, and no real name, SIN, address, or real wage appears on any tab.
